interviewQuestions.question: Why should the team invest time in accessibility work when it's competing against feature deadlines?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd lay out four separate arguments, because different people in the room respond to different ones, and leaning on just one tends to get discounted.

First, **scale**: the WHO estimates roughly 1 in 6 people globally have a significant disability, and that's before counting temporary impairments (a broken arm, eye surgery recovery) and situational ones (a parent holding a baby, someone in bright sunlight) that touch nearly everyone at some point — this isn't a niche user segment. Second, **legal exposure**: ADA web-accessibility litigation in the US alone runs into the thousands of filings a year, and courts have repeatedly held that public-accommodation requirements extend to websites, not just physical buildings — this is active risk, not a hypothetical. Third, the **curb-cut effect**: captions, keyboard shortcuts, high contrast, and plain language all end up benefiting far more users than the group they were built for, which changes the actual ROI calculation. Fourth, **cost asymmetry**: building accessibly from the start — semantic elements, contrast-checked color choices — is reliably cheaper than retrofitting after an audit or a complaint surfaces the gap, the same way any cross-cutting concern is cheaper to build in than bolt on.

I'd close by tying it to a concrete near-term ask — "our new checkout flow should ship keyboard-operable and screen-reader-tested from day one" — rather than leaving it as an abstract principle with no owner.

**Testing:** whether you can make the business case concretely, not just assert accessibility is 'the right thing to do' and hope that lands.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Someone on your team says "we don't need to worry about accessibility, we don't have blind users." How do you respond?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by not treating the claim as obviously false and dismissing it — I'd ask how they know that, because unless the product has explicit usage analytics tied to assistive technology (rare, and even then undercounted, since many users don't disclose it), the honest answer is usually "we don't actually know." Screen reader usage isn't the kind of thing that shows up in standard analytics.

Then I'd widen the frame beyond blindness specifically, since that's the single narrowest interpretation of accessibility: motor impairments affecting keyboard/mouse use, low vision needing higher contrast or zoom, situational impairments like a user in bright sunlight or holding a baby, temporary ones like a broken arm — these are all far more common than "totally blind," and none of them are captured by "we checked, no screen reader users."

I'd also point out the products the org depends on — vendor security questionnaires, enterprise procurement, and increasingly RFPs — often ask about WCAG conformance directly, regardless of whether the team believes it has affected users today, so the exposure exists even absent direct evidence either way.

I'd close with the curb-cut framing: most of this work — captions, contrast, keyboard operability — improves the experience for users who aren't disabled at all, so the downside of investing, even if the premise turns out to be wrong, is close to zero.

**Testing:** whether you can push back on a confidently wrong assumption professionally, with evidence and a wider frame, rather than either capitulating or getting defensive.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Communication

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between accessibility as a compliance checkbox and accessibility as a genuine product quality bar, and why does the distinction matter in practice?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Compliance-as-checkbox usually means "pass an automated audit tool and stop there" — running axe or a similar scanner, fixing whatever it flags, and considering the work done. The problem is automated tools catch roughly a third of real WCAG issues by most estimates; they're excellent at missing-alt-text and contrast-ratio failures, and structurally unable to catch things like "does this custom dropdown's keyboard interaction actually make sense" or "does this error message get announced at the right moment."

Treating accessibility as a genuine quality bar means the automated scan is a floor, not the finish line — it's followed by an actual keyboard-only pass through key flows and, ideally, a real screen-reader pass, the same way a product team wouldn't consider "it compiled" sufficient evidence that a feature works.

The practical difference shows up at exactly the failure mode I've seen most often: a team ships a 100% clean automated-audit score on a component whose custom modal still traps keyboard focus incorrectly or can't be closed with Escape — passing every automated check while being genuinely broken for a real user. Compliance framing optimizes for the audit; quality framing optimizes for the user, and the audit becomes one input among several rather than the definition of done.

**Testing:** whether you understand automated tooling's real limits, or would stop at a green checkmark and call the work finished.
